In summary, our research is concerned with
the stability analysis of pulse-coupling, a mechanism that is ubiquitous in neural circuits.
the study of the stability of dynamical states of networks of pulse-coulpled oscillators.
the stability of periodic states of pulse-coupling neural networks.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the stability of a periodic spiking activity is not only related to the smoothness of the phase-response curve but also to the shape of the post-synaptic potential.
the stability of the synchronous regime depends on the smoothness properties of both the phase response curve and the post-synaptic potential, and on the number of neurons in the network.
, in the absence of noise, a perfectly periodic state of a pulse-coupled network is always linearly stable.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the stability properties of pulse-coupling are not as straightforward as they might have appeared at first sight.
the mean-field approach, which is valid for a large class of systems, is not sufficient to predict stability of asynchronous states.
we have shown how to determine the stability of an arbitrary periodic state in a network of pulse-coupling oscillators, and we have shown that there are two classes of perturbation.
The main takeaway from our work is that

, for a given network of oscillators with a given connectivity and a given coupling function, the stability properties of a given dynamical regime depend not only on the mean-field properties of the regime, but also on its “microscopic” features.
the stability of a given regime is not a property of the network alone, but also of its environment.
, in the absence of a complete analytical solution, the stability of a dynamical state can be assessed through a combination of mean-field and “microscopic” analyses.
